The post Tencent WeVisOne-VL Unifies Detection, OCR, Segmentation and Matting appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> Tencent’s WeChat Vision team has released WeVisOne-VL , an open vision language model in 2B and 4B sizes. The WeVisOne-VL vision language model handles detection, referring, counting, pointing, OCR, segmentation and alpha matting in one model. Pixel outputs come from a 9.6M-parameter decoder, so no separate SAM is needed. It also answers “None” when a queried object is absent. For developers, that can replace a detector, an OCR engine and a segmenter with one model. TL;DR Size: 2B ( 2.44B params ) and 4B ( 4.83B params ) on Hugging Face, and a 9.6M-parameter pixel decoder. Trained with up to 8,192 tokens of context; deployment context length is not disclosed. Runs on: A single GPU through Transformers or vLLM in BF16. The package also lists NPU and CPU devices. VRAM needs are not disclosed. A community GGUF ran object-level tasks on a 6 GB RTX 2060. Performance: Beats the same-scale VLM baselines in Tencent’s tables on most of 30+ benchmarks (self-reported). Best: 71.3 F1 Mean on Dense200 dense detection, versus 58.7 for LocateAnything-3B. Worst: 52.6% rejection rate on PR-Bench, so many absent-target queries still get a box. What is WeVisOne-VL? WeVisOne-VL (“WeChat Vision All-in-One”) is a perception-focused model from Tencent built on Qwen3-VL . It targets fine-grained localization rather than open-ended chat. Users choose the output granularity: points, boxes, binary masks or continuous alpha mattes. How does WeVisOne-VL work? Every task is cast as structured next-token prediction. The model adds coordinate tokens <0> to <1000> for normalized boxes and points. An absent target produces None instead of a guessed box. For pixel tasks, the model emits an <OBJ> token after each predicted box. Its hidden state becomes a query for the pixel decoder, according to the model card . The decoder has 3 parts: Visual Feature Adapter: reuses multi-level Qwen3-VL ViT features instead of a second image encoder. Box-Guided Query Decoder: 6 deformable cross-attention blocks seeded by the <OBJ> state and the box. Dense Prediction Head: refines output at S/4, S/2 and S/1 into a full-resolution mask or matte. How was it trained? A knowledge-graph-driven data engine annotated over 100M images with about 3.6B boxes. SAM3, Rex-Omni and an in-house detector proposed regions, and Qwen3-VL verified them. Training used 3 SFT stages. Stage 1 aligned output formats on 90M examples. Stage 2 raised input to 1,960 visual tokens and up to 500 boxes per response. Stage 3 trained the pixel decoder, then specialized it for matting on 130M samples. A final GRPO stage used 178K uncertainty-filtered examples, as described in the research paper . How does WeVisOne-VL perform on benchmarks? All numbers below are self-reported, using greedy decoding and at most 1,960 visual tokens per image. Detection, referring and OCR use F1 averaged over IoU 0.5 to 0.95. Detection: 55.3 F1 on LVIS and 71.3 on Dense200 for the 4B model. Referring: 81.8 F1 on RefCOCOg test, versus 77.6 for LocateAnything-3B. Rejection: 96.4% on Tencent’s in-house WeRef-Bench (2,880 queries), versus 73.0%. Counting: 89.6% exact-match on PixMo-Count test, versus 82.8%. OCR: 52.0 F1 on TotalText, ahead of the PP-OCRv5 specialist at 25.7. Segmentation: 71.2 gIoU on ReasonSeg val, versus 65.0 for LISA-13B. Matting: 7.3 MAD on P3M-500-NP box prompts, versus 15.4 for SAM2-Matting (SAM3). Lower is better. The 2B model trails the 4B model on most tasks. It still scores better box-prompted matting on P3M-500-NP, at 6.6 MAD. Weights for the 2B and 4B models are on Hugging Face. The wevisone_vl package wraps Transformers and vLLM backends. The post webAI Releases TwIL-8B, an 8.8B Reasoning Model Scoring 98.2 on MATH-500 appeared first on MarkTechPost . ]]> webAI has released TwIL-8B , an 8.8B reasoning model for math, code and instruction following. The TwIL-8B reasoning model is post-trained from IBM’s Granite 4.2 8B . Weights are on Hugging Face under a non-commercial license. webAI’s launch post frames the pitch around cost per task, not raw scale. The 4-bit build is 4.98 GiB, sized for CPU or modest-VRAM GPU inference. TL;DR Size: 8.79B parameters, dense. 131,072-token context, inherited from the base model. Runs on: CPU or modest-VRAM GPU via a 4.98 GiB Q4_K_M GGUF. Full bf16 weights are 16.38 GiB. Performance: Leads its size class on math and code, trails on knowledge benchmarks. Best: MATH-500 at 98.2, the top score in webAI’s comparison. Worst: GPQA Diamond at 70.2, 11.5 points behind Qwen3.5-9B. HLE is 12.6 (verbose variant). What is TwIL-8B? TwIL-8B is a dense decoder-only reasoning model from webAI. It has 40 layers, hidden size 4096, and 32 attention heads with 8 KV heads . Input and output are English text only. The model writes a <think> block before each answer. It ships in 2 variants with the same architecture and tokenizer. Balanced is the default and produces shorter reasoning traces. Verbose reasons longer and targets hard contest-style problems. TwIL-8B extends webAI’s TwIL family. The first members were 1.7B and 3B formal-logic models released in August 2026. How was TwIL-8B trained? webAI used 3 post-training stages : Full-parameter SFT on reasoning traces for math, STEM and instruction following. GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning on math, code, STEM and instruction prompts. This produces the verbose variant. Length-aware RL with a reward that favors shorter traces against per-domain length references. This produces the balanced variant. Training pools were decontaminated with 13-gram matching against AIME, HMMT, MATH-500, GPQA and other evals. How does TwIL-8B perform on benchmarks? All TwIL-8B scores are self-reported, high-effort pass@1 with thinking enabled. Scores marked † were measured on the verbose variant only. Math : TwIL-8B scores 98.2 on MATH-500. Qwen3.5-9B lists 96.6 on a third-party leaderboard . Gemma 4 31B scored 87.9 in Red Hat’s lighteval run . On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B posts 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On AIME 2026 it scores 88.3, behind Qwen3.5-9B at 92.5 and Gemma 4 31B at 89.2 . Code : LiveCodeBench† is 81.6, against 65.6 for Qwen3.5-9B and 80.0 for Gemma 4 31B. webAI notes its LiveCodeBench version was not recorded. Competitor scores are v6. Instruction following : IFBench† is 74.4, 9.9 points above Qwen3.5-9B at 64.5. IFEval is level, at 91.8 vs 91.5. Knowledge : This is the weak spot. GPQA Diamond is 70.2, against 81.7 for Qwen3.5-9B and 84.3 for Gemma 4 31B. MMLU-Pro† is 76.5 vs 82.5 for Qwen3.5-9B. Across 13 shared benchmarks, TwIL-8B goes 7-6 against Qwen3.5-9B. Against Gemma 4 31B, about 3.5x its size, it goes 3-11. Does TwIL-8B use fewer reasoning tokens? Yes, against its closest open peer. On AIME 2026, TwIL-8B averages about 19.5k output tokens per problem. Qwen3.5-9B uses 31.2k, so TwIL-8B uses 38% fewer. It scores 4.2 points lower. On HMMT Feb 2026 the gap is 32.9k vs 40.6k, or 19% fewer. Frontier models remain far leaner. webAI cites about 5k tokens per AIME 2026 problem for GPT-5.5. webAI states that harnesses and tokenizers differ, so treat this as directional. Together Compiler already runs on several of Together’s serverless endpoints. The core claim for developers: an engine tuned once goes stale, so tuning should never stop. TL;DR System: It is an optimization system, tested on Kimi K3, GLM 5.3, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, DeepSeek v4.1 Flash and Llama 1B. Runs on: NVIDIA B200, B300, GB300, H100, AMD MI355X and AWS Trainium2. Each run used at most 2 nodes per model. Performance: Up to 2.6x higher TPS than the best published InferenceX configurations, in under 24 hours per setting. Best: 1,111 P90 TPS per user on MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200, batch size 1), 1.8x over the 633 TPS baseline. Worst: GLM 5.3 on MI355X moved only from 463 to 480 TPS (about 4%). What is Together Compiler? Together Compiler is a continual compilation loop from Together AI that uses coding agents to rewrite a model’s forward pass. It takes a server launch command, a traffic profile and a hardware configuration. Agents propose faster forward passes, and a persistent engine measures each one. The winning code ships into the serving engine. When traffic drifts, the loop runs again. Why does inference need continual compilation? Together AI team reports that its traffic shape never sits still. Prompt lengths in one country ran about 97K tokens versus 70K elsewhere. One customer’s P90 input length grew from 18K to 33K tokens in 3 days. Kernels tuned on random data can also mislead. Random inputs activated 13 to 38% more MoE experts than real traffic. One agent-written top-k kernel took 20 µs on random data. On real data at 70K context, it took up to 62 ms. How does the persistent engine work? Most agent loops restart vLLM, SGLang or TensorRT-LLM for every experiment. The research team measures 761 seconds of cold startup for MiniMax M3.1 Flash on TensorRT-LLM. Together Compiler starts the engine once. Agents submit a candidate forward pass over RPC. The server swaps the forward function pointer and re-captures CUDA graphs. Two measurement tiers balance speed and fidelity. A fast tier serves 12 layers for quick screening. A slow tier serves 60 layers to confirm gains on real distributions. Two tiers tested 8.1x more candidates than one slow tier (1,354 vs 168). They also found a solution 7.2% faster. Together AI team reports 252x higher agent experiment throughput than an engine-restart baseline. How does it choose a parallelism layout? A cost model ranks tensor, expert, data and context parallel layouts before agents start. It mixes spec-sheet numbers, microbenchmarks and measured forward passes. It also uses measured MoE expert imbalance and uneven request lengths. On Kimi K3, it found a production layout with up to 24% higher TPS. What did agents need from human experts? An expert-curated knowledge base produced 25 to 31% lower speedup after 12 hours. Naive agents told to make the forward pass “as fast as possible” beat expert strategies. The ensemble scores were 6.2x versus 4.9x after 10 trials. Custom logging structures ate up to 43% of tool calls. Together AI now gives agents raw engine source code, not an intermediate representation. Benchmarks: how fast is Together Compiler? On SemiAnalysis InferenceX ‘s AgentX workload, Together Compiler beat the best open configurations by up to 2.6x TPS. Each setting ran under 24 hours on at most 2 nodes. Batch size 1, P90 TPS per user (Together Compiler vs InferenceX best, self-reported): MiniMax M3.1 Flash (B200): 1,111 vs 633 DeepSeek v4.1 Flash (GB300): 1,205 vs 943 GLM 5.3 (B200): 417 vs 329 Kimi K3 (GB300): 450 vs 423 GLM 5.3 (MI355X): 480 vs 463 For MiniMax, the cost model picked TP8 over the baseline’s TP4. That halves each GPU’s weight traffic in memory-bound decode. On Llama 1B at batch size 1, it beat Hazy Research megakernels , Mirage and CUDA-graph baselines by up to 1.7x.
